questions.q: What is platform engineering's core responsibility, as recapped in this lesson?
options: Running the error budget policy and deciding when a feature freeze applies
Writing postmortems after every production incident
Building and maintaining the self-service 'paved road' — standardized tools, templates, and provisioning systems with sensible defaults
Approving marketing copy for new product launches
questions.explain: Platform engineering's job is the paved road itself: the self-service systems and templates that let teams get sensible infrastructure defaults without needing deep infra expertise of their own.

questions.q: Why is it inaccurate to describe SRE and platform engineering as 'just two names for the same job,' per this lesson?
options: Because SRE only exists in companies that don't have a platform team

Because platform engineering builds and maintains the paved road itself, while SRE is responsible for the reliability of what actually runs on that road — a service can run on a well-built paved road and still have a bad SLO
Because platform engineers are not allowed to write code
Because SRE has no connection whatsoever to infrastructure
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes the two by responsibility: platform engineering owns the road itself; SRE owns SLOs, error budget policy, incident response, and toil reduction for what runs on it. A good road doesn't guarantee a good SLO.

questions.q: According to this lesson, how does SRE achieve standardized SLO practice across hundreds of services without enforcing it team by team through persuasion alone?
options: By mandating that every team hire its own dedicated SRE
By getting its reliability requirements built directly into the platform's default templates, so every new service inherits observability, canary steps, and a standard SLO config automatically
By banning any team from launching a new service
By outsourcing all SLO tracking to a third-party vendor
questions.explain: The leverage point is the paved road itself: when SRE's requirements are baked into the platform's defaults, standardization becomes something every team gets for free, rather than something SRE has to enforce individually.

questions.q: Why does baking SRE's reliability requirements into the platform's default templates also function as a toil-reduction strategy?
options: It eliminates the need for any SLOs at all
It has no connection to toil reduction; it is purely a standardization tactic
Because it increases the manual setup work required of each new team
Baking a reliability default into the platform once removes a piece of manual, repetitive setup work that every team would otherwise have had to do for itself
questions.explain: This connects back to Lesson 3's definition of toil: building observability or a canary step into the platform once, instead of every team doing it manually and repeatedly, removes exactly the kind of repetitive manual work that defines toil.

questions.q: What are the two structural approaches this lesson describes for organizing the SRE/platform-engineering relationship at scale?
options: Either team can be eliminated entirely once a company reaches enterprise scale

A dedicated, centralized platform team with SRE as a close consulting partner whose requirements get embedded into platform defaults, or a combined 'Platform SRE' function owning both responsibilities under one roof
Platform engineering must always report directly to the marketing department
SRE and platform engineering must always be the exact same group of individual engineers
questions.explain: The lesson names two working structures: a centralized platform team with SRE embedding requirements into its defaults as a consulting partner, or a combined Platform SRE function owning both the paved road and its reliability guarantees.
